patterns.usage_note: Names an explicit yardstick and then reports a result that clashes with it, so the payload of the sentence is the 'and yet': 新人にしては says the newcomer standard has been overshot, not merely met. That counter-expectation is what puts it beside くせして and わりにゃ here; the same string is filed in the 話題-提示 class when it is only setting the frame the comment is relative to. The standard has to be something nameable, so it hooks straight onto a bare noun where its sibling わりに needs の first, and unlike わりに it is not normally used after a plain i-adjective. にしちゃ is the clipped conversational realization, にしては the everyday one, and にしましては the ます-polite realization heard in formal service speech.

examples.ruby: 一日[いちにち]で仕上[しあ]げたにしては、上出来[じょうでき]だと思[おも]う。
examples.english: For something finished in a single day, I'd say it came out well.

examples.ruby: 彼[かれ]は新人[しんじん]にしては度胸[どきょう]が据[す]わっている。
examples.english: He's remarkably unflappable for a first-year hire.

examples.ruby: 三月[さんがつ]にしちゃ、ずいぶん風[かぜ]が冷[つめ]たいね。
examples.english: Pretty biting wind for March, isn't it.

patterns.usage_note: Weighs a result against the degree the first clause would lead you to expect, so it takes gradable material — i-adjectives, past events with a measurable amount, or a noun of scale via の (値段の割に). That i-adjective slot is what separates it from にしては, and unlike くせに it carries no reproach, only a mild 'more/less than you'd think'. Keep it apart from the homophonous adverb 割に / 割と ('fairly, comparatively', as in 割に寒い), which is a separate word; わりにゃ is the clipped spoken realization and 割に the ordinary written one.

examples.ruby: この店[みせ]は狭[せま]い割[わり]に品揃[しなぞろ]えが豊富[ほうふ]だ。
examples.english: For such a cramped shop, it carries a surprising range.

examples.ruby: 五[ご]キロも走[はし]った割[わり]に、まったく疲[つか]れていない。
examples.english: Considering I ran five kilometers, I'm not tired in the slightest.

examples.ruby: 値段[ねだん]の割[わり]に、この鞄[かばん]は縫[ぬ]い目[め]が粗[あら]い。
examples.english: For what it costs, the stitching on this bag is sloppy.

patterns.usage_note: The reproachful member of this group: the speaker is criticizing, mocking or looking down on someone whose behavior clashes with what they are. Teaching references state the restriction that both clauses must share a subject, and that subject is normally a person, which is why くせに cannot simply be swapped in for every のに. It attaches to a noun through の (子供のくせに) and to a na-adjective through な; くせして is the blunter, more colloquial realization of くせに and is best avoided about anyone senior to you.

examples.ruby: 本当[ほんとう]は知[し]っているくせに、何[なに]も教[おし]えてくれない。
examples.english: He knows perfectly well, and yet he won't tell me a thing.

examples.ruby: 彼[かれ]は毎回[まいかい]遅[おく]れてくるくせして、平気[へいき]な顔[かお]をしている。
examples.english: He turns up late every single time and still has the nerve to look unbothered.

examples.ruby: 子供[こども]のくせに、ずいぶん大人[おとな]びた口[くち]をきく。
examples.english: Quite the grown-up way of talking, for a kid.
